items.prompt: A rectangular maze allows orthogonal movement between open cells. Which graph mapping is the correct starting model?

options.text: Each row is one vertex, because cells in a row share a coordinate.
Cell values are vertices and coordinates are edges.
Each open cell is a vertex, with an edge to each in-bounds open orthogonal neighbor.
Each cell has one parent edge because any maze can be treated as a tree.

feedback.reason: The state is the current open coordinate, and legal one-step moves define the edges.

blocks.text: Coordinates are states and legal moves are edges

items: Treat each open coordinate (r,c) as one vertex.
For offsets (−1,0), (1,0), (0,−1), and (0,1), compute a candidate coordinate.
Create an implicit edge only when the candidate is in bounds and open.
Use BFS or DFS over those generated neighbors according to the requested output.

blocks.text: A row cannot be one vertex because obstacles and vertical connections differ by column. Cell values alone also lose position, and maze adjacency may contain cycles, so a single parent is a traversal result rather than the input graph.

blocks.title: Grid mapping
blocks.text: Use the smallest state that determines all legal future moves; in this static maze it is the open coordinate.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.rows_vertices: Cells in one row can have different obstacles and different legal neighbors, so collapsing the row loses state.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.values_edges: Two cells with the same value can occupy different positions and have different neighborhoods; coordinates identify the states here.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.tree_cells: Open-cell adjacency can contain cycles and multiple routes, so a parent relation is a traversal result rather than the input graph.

items.prompt: A cell is blocked by the input maze. How should that fact differ from a cell that is open but already visited by the current traversal?

options.text: They are semantically identical, so one permanent flag should represent both without distinction.
Blocked means the state or transition is illegal in the graph; visited means a legal state has already been discovered in this traversal.
A cell becomes blocked only when dequeued; this is equivalent to visited-on-enqueue.
Only an adjacency matrix can distinguish blocked from visited cells.

feedback.reason: Obstacle legality defines the graph; visited state records one traversal's progress through that graph.

blocks.text: Legality and traversal progress answer different questions

items: Blocked is immutable problem data: entering that coordinate is not a legal transition.
Visited is execution state: the coordinate is legal, but this traversal already discovered its corresponding state.
A second query may need the same open cell to begin unseen while the obstacle remains blocked.

blocks.text: Conflating the roles can destroy the original maze, prevent independent queries, or hide whether failure came from an obstacle or prior discovery. In-place marking is only an implementation of visited when mutation is allowed and the marker cannot collide with any meaningful input value.

blocks.title: Ownership rule
blocks.text: Obstacles belong to the graph definition; visited belongs to one traversal.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_flag: Obstacles belong to the problem instance, while visited state is execution-specific and may need to be reset or queried separately.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.blocked_after_dequeue: Whether a cell is an obstacle is known before traversal and is not a frontier-timing decision.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.matrix_only: A grid plus a separate visited structure or safe in-place marker can represent the distinction directly.

items.prompt: The same occupied-cell grid is evaluated once with 4-direction adjacency and once with 8-direction adjacency. Which part of the graph model changes?

options.text: Only the visited timing changes; graph edges are identical.
Using BFS instead of DFS adds the diagonal edges because BFS is broader.
A grid cannot represent two adjacency rules without converting to an adjacency matrix.
The vertex set can remain the same, but diagonal legal moves add edges in the 8-direction model.

feedback.reason: The movement rule is the edge relation, so adding diagonals changes connectivity and distances.

blocks.text: The neighborhood rule is the edge relation

Cells (0,0) and (1,1) share only a corner. Four-direction offsets create no edge between them; adding diagonal offsets in the eight-direction model creates one. The candidate vertex set is unchanged, but connectivity and shortest distances may change.

blocks.title: Traversal does not define adjacency
blocks.text: BFS and DFS explore the edges supplied by the movement contract. Neither visited timing nor traversal breadth can legalize a forbidden diagonal.

blocks.title: Model first
blocks.text: Declare directions, wraparound, portals and corner-cutting rules before selecting or analyzing traversal.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.visited_changes_edges: Visited timing cannot make a diagonal transition legal when the movement contract forbids it.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.bfs_changes_graph: Traversal order explores a fixed graph; it does not define its legal transitions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.representation_invalid: Neighbor generation can use a four-direction or eight-direction offset table on the same grid.

items.prompt: A grid traversal may overwrite an open cell with a visited marker. Select all conditions needed for that in-place choice to preserve the problem contract.

options.text: The grid must be a tree, otherwise in-place marking is invalid.
The caller permits the grid to be mutated or no later consumer needs the original values.
Visited must be written only on dequeue because enqueue-time marking changes the grid too early.
The chosen marker cannot be confused with any meaningful unvisited cell value.

feedback.reason: In-place visited storage is safe only when mutation is allowed and the marker has a distinct meaning.

blocks.text: In-place visited storage changes an external contract

items: Mutation must be permitted, or no later consumer may need the original grid values.
The marker must be outside the domain of every meaningful unvisited cell value.
Neighbor logic must consistently recognize the marker as already discovered rather than as a new cell type.

blocks.text: A separate boolean grid preserves the input; in-place mutation can save that storage but consumes information. Cycles do not make mutation invalid, and BFS normally writes the marker at enqueue time to prevent duplicate scheduling.

blocks.title: Trade-off
blocks.text: Use in-place marking only when mutation and marker semantics are both safe.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.tree_guarantee: In-place marking is a storage choice and works on cyclic grid graphs when discovery timing is correct.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.dequeue_required: For BFS, marking when a legal cell is first enqueued usually prevents duplicate scheduling and remains semantically valid.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.mutation_allowed: Destroying input that must be reused violates an external contract even if the traversal result is correct.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.marker_unambiguous: A colliding marker can make an unvisited legal cell appear blocked or already processed.

items.prompt: A robot may break at most one wall. It can reach cell (r,c) before using the break and later reach the same cell after using it, with different future options. What is the correct graph-state identity?

options.text: (r, c) only, because every physical cell is one graph vertex in every grid problem.
breakUsed only, because coordinates are merely visual layout.
(r, c, breakUsed), so the two arrivals are distinct vertices in the implicit graph.
No visited structure, because revisiting cells is required.

feedback.reason: A graph vertex must include the resource bit because it changes which outgoing moves remain legal.

blocks.text: One physical cell can represent two search vertices

items: State (r,c,false) can move into an adjacent wall and transition to (nextR,nextC,true).
State (r,c,true) cannot spend the wall break again.
Because their outgoing legal moves differ, visited must distinguish the two states.

blocks.text: Coordinate-only visited can discard an arrival that still owns the break and may be the only route to the goal. Break state alone loses location. The implicit graph has at most 2RC states, and revisiting a coordinate under the other resource bit is not an uncontrolled duplicate.

blocks.title: State rule
blocks.text: Include history exactly when it changes future transitions or costs.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.coordinate_only: The remaining wall-break capability changes future legal transitions, so collapsing the states can discard the optimal or only valid route.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.break_only: Movement and destination depend on location; resource state alone is insufficient.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.no_visited: Revisiting a coordinate under a different resource state is handled by a richer key, not by allowing unlimited duplicate states.

items.prompt: An open-cell grid has unit-cost orthogonal moves, and the output is the minimum number of moves from start to goal. After mapping the grid to a graph, which traversal property is decisive?

options.text: The first DFS route is minimum because DFS reaches a goal before BFS finishes a layer.
BFS processes states by nondecreasing number of unit edges, so first discovery gives the minimum move count.
An adjacency matrix makes either traversal return the shortest path automatically.
Minimum distance requires marking every cell only on dequeue, which is always equivalent.

feedback.reason: The grid mapping produces an unweighted graph, and BFS layer number equals path length in moves.

blocks.text: Move count is unweighted graph distance

items: Place start in BFS layer 0.
Every legal orthogonal move adds one edge, so neighbors of layer d receive distance d + 1.
FIFO processing exhausts layer d before any layer d + 1 state is expanded.
Therefore the first discovery of goal has the minimum possible move count.

blocks.text: DFS can prove reachability but may follow a longer route first. A matrix changes neighbor lookup, not exploration order. If terrain moves have unequal costs, layer number no longer equals objective cost and the frontier must change to a weighted shortest-path discipline.

blocks.title: Traversal boundary
blocks.text: Use BFS first discovery for minimum move count only when every legal move has equal cost.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.dfs_first_path: DFS discovery order is not ordered by path length and can find a long route first.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.matrix_shortest: Representation affects neighbor access but does not give DFS a shortest-path guarantee.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mark_dequeue: Discovery-time marking with distance assignment is the standard one-enqueue invariant for unit-cost BFS.

items.prompt: For an R × C grid with at most four generated neighbors per cell, why is a full adjacency matrix normally a poor traversal representation?

options.text: A matrix cannot represent grid edges correctly under any conditions.
Because BFS is always faster than DFS and therefore forbids matrices.
Because marking visited on dequeue generates all needed edges without a movement rule.
There are O(RC) states and O(RC) local edges, while a matrix over all cells uses O((RC)²) space.

feedback.reason: Grid geometry provides O(1) neighbor generation per state, so quadratic all-pairs storage adds no useful index.

blocks.text: Bounded degree keeps the implicit graph linear

items: Flattening an R × C grid gives N = RC possible cell vertices.
At most four candidates are generated per cell, so total neighbor checks and edges are O(4N) = O(N).
Traversal plus visited/frontier storage is therefore O(RC), aside from the input grid.

blocks.text: An adjacency matrix has N rows and N columns, using O(N²) = O((RC)²) space even though almost every pair of cells is nonadjacent. It is mathematically capable of storing the graph, but on-demand direction checks provide the needed index directly.

blocks.title: Representation rule
blocks.text: For a bounded-degree grid, generate edges in O(1) per state instead of materializing all cell pairs.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.matrix_incorrect: It can represent them, but it stores overwhelmingly many absent cell-to-cell edges for a bounded-degree grid.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.bfs_only_reason: Both traversals can consume either representation; the issue is the grid's sparse implicit edge structure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.visited_replaces_edges: Visited state does not define which neighboring coordinates are legal.

items.prompt: Select all checks required before enqueuing a candidate cell while generating implicit grid neighbors.

options.text: The row and column are within the grid bounds.
The cell satisfies the problem's traversability rule, such as not being blocked.
The relevant graph-state identity has not already been visited.
The coordinate is lexicographically larger than the current cell.

feedback.reason: Implicit edges are legal only when the neighbor exists, is traversable, and represents new state.

blocks.text: Bounds and obstacle checks implement the grid's edge relation. Visited state prevents cycles and duplicate work; for augmented states it must include the extra resource such as remaining wall breaks. Coordinate order is not a movement legality rule.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorted_coordinate: Movement is defined by allowed directions and cell properties, not lexical coordinate order.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.open_cell: Blocked cells are not traversable vertices under the stated rule.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.unvisited_state: Revisiting a state can cause cycles or repeated work.

items.prompt: A robot can break one wall. It reaches the same cell once with the break unused and once with it used. Why are those not the same graph state?

options.text: Future reachability differs, so the state identity must include the cell and remaining break budget.
The coordinate uniquely determines future options, so one visited bit is enough.
The entire path must be stored because no finite state can represent the budget.
Track one global wall count shared by all paths to the cell.

feedback.reason: A resource used by future transitions is part of the vertex identity in the expanded graph.

blocks.text: At the same (r,c), a path with one break remaining can enter a wall that a path with zero cannot. Marking the coordinate alone would discard the stronger state. The entire path is unnecessary because position plus remaining budget summarizes the future relevant information.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.cell_only: Different remaining budgets lead to different legal neighbors.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.path_string: The path history is more detail than the transition needs once the budget is included.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.wall_count_global: Each path has its own remaining budget; one global counter conflates independent states.

items.prompt: When is overwriting open grid cells with a visited marker a safe alternative to a separate visited matrix?

options.text: When input mutation is allowed, the marker cannot collide with legal cell values, and no later phase needs the original grid distinction.
Always, because traversal never needs the input after the first read.
Whenever any value is available, even if it is a legal unvisited cell value.
Never; graph traversal must always allocate a separate visited matrix.

feedback.reason: In-place visitation is a representation optimization constrained by mutation, marker collision, and downstream-read contracts.

blocks.text: Overwriting can reduce auxiliary space, but it destroys the original cell value. The contract must permit that side effect, the marker must remain distinguishable, and any later logic must not need the original grid. Otherwise a separate visited structure or a copy is required.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_safe: Later consumers may need the original grid, and mutation may be forbidden.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.marker_any_value: A legal unvisited cell with the same value could be mistaken for visited.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.copy_required: A separate matrix is safe but not the only legal implementation when the stated conditions hold.

items.prompt: What changes when a grid problem defines connectivity using four directions instead of eight?

options.text: Diagonal cells are not neighbors and must not be traversed as one step.
Every touching cell, including diagonals, remains connected.
Only horizontal moves are legal.
Only vertical moves are legal.

feedback.reason: The direction set is the graph's edge contract.

blocks.text: Use offsets (-1,0),(1,0),(0,-1),(0,1) for four-neighbor connectivity. Adding diagonal offsets silently changes components and path lengths.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.row_only: Vertical moves are also legal in the four-direction contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.column_only: Horizontal moves are also legal in the four-direction contract.

items.prompt: When generating a neighbor row nr and column nc in a grid, what must happen before reading grid[nr][nc]?

options.text: Check 0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols before indexing.
Read the cell first and check bounds afterward.
Clamp every out-of-range coordinate to the nearest border cell.
Ignore bounds because the direction list is finite.

feedback.reason: The coordinate must be validated before it becomes an array access.

blocks.text: Clamping creates artificial self-edges at borders; reading first can raise an invalid-access error. Boundary checks are part of grid graph construction.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.read_then_check: The invalid read has already occurred.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.clamp: Clamping changes the intended neighbor relation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ignore: Finite directions still produce out-of-range coordinates at borders.

items.prompt: For a grid with C columns, which mapping uniquely flattens cell (r,c) into a row-major vertex id?

options.text: r*C + c.
r + c.
r*R + c, using the number of rows as the stride.
r*C*c, which preserves no unique row boundary.

feedback.reason: Each completed row contributes C positions before column c is added.

blocks.text: The inverse is row=id/C and column=id%C. The stride is the number of columns, not rows, because rows are laid out contiguously.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.column_only: Different cells such as (0,1) and (1,0) collide.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.wrong_stride: Using rows as stride is incorrect for row-major storage when R differs from C.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.product_only: Multiplication by c does not encode each column as an offset.

items.prompt: How should an impassable grid cell be treated in a traversal-as-graph model?

options.text: Treat it as unavailable state and do not enqueue or traverse through it.
Enqueue it like every open cell and filter only after traversal.
Use it as a traversal source because obstacles connect regions.
Add edges from it to every open cell.

feedback.reason: Obstacle semantics remove the cell from the traversable graph or block all incident transitions.

blocks.text: Allowing an obstacle into the queue creates paths through forbidden space and can merge components that should remain separate.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_vertex: Post-filtering cannot undo incorrect reachability through an obstacle.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.source_only: Obstacles are blocked states, not sources.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.teleport: Teleport edges contradict local grid adjacency.
